questions.question_text:
In this pattern each row is the row above divided by $t$.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Power} & \text{Value}\\\hline t^{0} & 1\\ t^{-1} & \frac{1}{t}\\ t^{-2} & \frac{1}{t^{2}}\\ t^{-3} & ?\end{array}$
Continuing the pattern, what is $t^{-3}$ with a positive index?

options.why: Reads the negative index as a negative sign on the power instead of continuing the divide-by-$t$ pattern.
Makes the index positive without moving the base to the denominator, ignoring the pattern's division.
Treats the index as a multiplier of the base, giving $3t$ in the denominator rather than three factors of $t$.

questions.question_text: Simplifying $\frac{p^{4}}{p^{7}}$ with the index law of division and again by cancelling common factors establishes which result?

options.why: Cancels using the numerator's index, leaving four factors below instead of the difference of the indices.
Reads the negative index as a negative sign, so the cancelled form is written as the opposite of $p^{3}$.
Subtracts the indices in the wrong order, giving $7-4$ instead of $4-7$ from the division law.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{p^{4}}{p^{7}}$
$=p^{4-7}$
$=p^{-3}$
$\frac{p^{4}}{p^{7}}=\frac{1}{p^{3}}$ after cancelling the four common factors
$p^{-3}=\frac{1}{p^{3}}$

questions.question_text: Use the index law of powers to write $x^{-4}$ as a power raised to $-1$, then take its reciprocal. Which working establishes the correct result?

options.why: Uses $x^3$ instead of $x^4$ as the inner power; $(x^3)^{-1}=x^{-3}$, not $x^{-4}$.
Treats raising $x^{4}$ to $-1$ as changing its sign instead of taking its reciprocal.
Treats the power $x^{4}$ as $4x$ when taking the reciprocal.

questions.solution_text:
$\left(x^{4}\right)^{-1}$
$=x^{4\times(-1)}$
$=x^{-4}$
Raising to the index $-1$ takes the reciprocal, so
$x^{-4}=\frac{1}{x^{4}}$

questions.question_text: Simplify $\frac{w^{3}}{w^{8}}$ using the division law and again by cancelling common factors. Which result do the two simplifications establish?

options.why: Treats the negative index as a minus sign on $w^{5}$ instead of taking its reciprocal.
Uses the numerator's index $3$ as the number of factors left below instead of subtracting $3$ from $8$.
Subtracts the indices in the wrong order, using $8-3$ instead of $3-8$.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{w^{3}}{w^{8}}$
$=w^{3-8}$
$=w^{-5}$
Cancelling the three common factors of $w$ leaves five factors of $w$ in the denominator, so
$\frac{w^{3}}{w^{8}}=\frac{1}{w^{5}}$
Therefore, $w^{-5}=\frac{1}{w^{5}}$.

questions.question_text: Use fraction division to show what $\frac{1}{n^{-4}}$ equals. Which working is correct?

options.why: Multiplies by the fraction being divided by instead of by its reciprocal.
Rewrites the negative index as a minus sign on $n^{4}$ instead of as a reciprocal.

questions.question_text:
A student writes $\frac{c^{2}}{c^{6}}=c^{2-6}=c^{-4}$, then $\frac{c^{2}}{c^{6}}=\frac{1}{c^{4}}$ by cancelling, and concludes $c^{-4}=-c^{4}$.
Which statement identifies the error?

options.text: The conclusion is wrong: the two simplifications must be equal, so $c^{-4}=\frac{1}{c^{4}}$.
The first line is wrong: $c^{2-6}$ should be $c^{-3}$.
options.why: Counts the gap between the indices $2$ and $6$ instead of subtracting them.

options.text: The cancelling line is wrong: it should leave $\frac{1}{c^{3}}$.
options.why: Cancels one factor too many, leaving three factors of $c$ below instead of four.

options.text: The conclusion is wrong: the two simplifications give $c^{-4}=c^{4}$.
options.why: Equates the two forms but drops the reciprocal, reading $\frac{1}{c^{4}}$ as $c^{4}$.

questions.solution_text:
Both simplifications describe the same expression, so their results must be equal.
$c^{-4}=\frac{1}{c^{4}}$
The negative index makes the reciprocal of $c^{4}$, not its opposite.

options.text: A negative index means the reciprocal of $a^{5}$, so $a^{-5}=\frac{1}{a^{5}}$.
A negative index means the opposite of the reciprocal, so $a^{-5}=-\frac{1}{a^{5}}$.
options.why: Applies the reciprocal and then also carries the index's minus sign onto the result.

options.text: They are only different when $a$ is negative; for positive $a$ the two are equal.
options.why: Assumes the rule depends on the sign of the base rather than holding for every $a\neq0$.

options.text: A negative index means multiply the base by the index, so $a^{-5}=-5a$.
options.why: Reads the index as a multiplier rather than as repeated multiplication.

questions.solution_text:
$a^{5}\times a^{-5}$
$=a^{0}$
$=1$
A product of $1$ makes $a^{-5}$ the reciprocal of $a^{5}$, so
$a^{-5}=\frac{1}{a^{5}}$

questions.question_text: Why does the $7$ in $7b^{-3}$ stay in the numerator when the term is written as $\frac{7}{b^{3}}$?

options.text: Only $b$ carries the index $-3$, so only $b$ is reciprocated.
The $7$ is a numeral, and numerals are never reciprocated.
options.why: Uses the type of number to decide rather than what the index is attached to, so $(7b)^{-3}$ would be handled wrongly too.

options.text: The $7$ would move only if the index were $-1$.
options.why: Ties the coefficient's fate to the size of the index instead of to whether brackets include it in the base.

options.text: The $7$ was already in the numerator, and rewriting never moves a numerator.
options.why: A negative index on an entire bracketed base, such as $(7b)^{-3}$, reciprocates the coefficient too: $(7b)^{-3}=\frac{1}{343b^{3}}$.

questions.solution_text:
$7b^{-3}$
$=7\times\frac{1}{b^{3}}$
$=\frac{7}{b^{3}}$
The index $-3$ is attached to $b$ alone, so the coefficient is untouched.

questions.question_text: Using $a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^{n}}$, what does $\frac{1}{d^{-5}}$ simplify to, and why?

options.text: $d^{5}$, because dividing $1$ by $\frac{1}{d^{5}}$ multiplies by the reciprocal $d^{5}$.
$\frac{1}{d^{5}}$, because the index becomes positive where it stands.
options.why: Makes the index positive without moving the base across the fraction line, so the reciprocal is taken only once.

options.text: $-d^{5}$, because the index's minus sign carries through to the result.
options.why: Keeps the minus sign of the index as a sign on the answer instead of as an instruction to reciprocate.

options.text: $5d$, because the index moves out in front of the base.
options.why: Reads the index as a coefficient of the base rather than as a power.

questions.question_text: Simplifying $\frac{x^{4}}{x^{9}}$ with the division law, and again by cancelling common factors, establishes which result?

options.why: Cancels using the numerator index $4$ instead of the $5$ factors of $x$ left in the denominator.
Reads the negative index produced by the division law as a negative sign on the power.
Subtracts the indices in the wrong order, giving $9-4$ instead of $4-9$.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{x^{4}}{x^{9}}$
$=x^{4-9}$
$=x^{-5}$
Cancelling the $4$ common factors of $x$ leaves $5$ factors of $x$ in the denominator, so $\frac{x^{4}}{x^{9}}=\frac{1}{x^{5}}$
$x^{-5}=\frac{1}{x^{5}}$
